items.prompt: What does 'concurrency' mean, as this unit defines it?
choices: Multiple tasks making progress over the same period of time, without necessarily executing at the exact same instant
Multiple tasks always executing at the literal same instant
A single task running as fast as possible
A guarantee that no task will ever wait for another
items.explanation: Concurrency only requires that tasks take turns and interleave — it doesn't require literal simultaneous execution, which is what parallelism specifically means.
items.reference:
Concurrency
progress over the same period
not necessarily the same instant

Why: Interleaving turns is enough for concurrency — true simultaneity is a separate, stronger property.

items.prompt: A single-threaded server handles 1,000 concurrent connections. Does this mean 1,000 pieces of JavaScript are executing at the same literal instant?
choices: No — the single thread takes turns between them; only one piece of JavaScript ever executes at a time
Yes, that's exactly what 'concurrent connections' means
Yes, but only if the server has multiple CPU cores
No, it means only one connection is actually being handled at all
items.explanation: A single thread can only run one thing at a time — concurrency here comes from rapidly interleaving turns between many pending callbacks, not from simultaneous execution.
items.reference:
Concurrency
progress over the same period
not necessarily the same instant

Why: Interleaving turns is enough for concurrency — true simultaneity is a separate, stronger property.

items.prompt: What's the minimum requirement for two tasks to be considered 'concurrent' with each other?
choices: They make progress over the same overall period of time, even if they take turns rather than running simultaneously
They must run on separate CPU cores
They must both finish at the exact same millisecond
They must be written in the same programming language
items.explanation: Concurrency is about overlapping progress over a period of time, not about literal simultaneous execution — that distinction is what separates it from parallelism.
items.reference:
Concurrency
progress over the same period

items.prompt: What is 'parallelism,' as distinct from concurrency?
choices: Tasks actually executing at the exact same instant, which requires more than one thread or core
Any situation involving more than one pending request
The same thing as concurrency, just a more formal name for it
A guarantee that a task will finish faster than expected
items.explanation: Parallelism specifically requires simultaneous execution — genuinely needing multiple threads or cores — which concurrency alone doesn't require.
items.reference:
Parallelism
same literal instant
requires multiple threads/cores

Why: Concurrency doesn't require parallelism, though the two terms are often used loosely as if they were synonyms.

Yes, concurrency is impossible without multiple CPU cores

No, concurrency and parallelism are unrelated concepts with nothing in common
items.explanation: A single-threaded event loop achieves real concurrency (many tasks making progress over time) with zero parallelism (never two tasks at the same instant).

items.prompt: What does 'blocking' mean, as this unit uses the term?
choices: Code that holds the current thread until it finishes, during which nothing else on that thread can make progress
Any code that takes longer than 100ms to run
Code that intentionally rejects incoming requests
A network error that prevents a request from completing
items.explanation: Blocking specifically means occupying the thread completely — even a queued, ready-to-run callback has to wait until the blocking code releases the thread.
items.reference:
Blocking
holds the thread until finished
nothing else on that thread can run meanwhile

Why: This is why a synchronous CPU-heavy calculation freezes everything else on a single-threaded server.

items.prompt: What is the event loop, as this unit describes it?
choices: The mechanism a single-threaded runtime uses to interleave many pending callbacks, giving each a turn between yields
A hardware component that runs JavaScript in parallel
A loop that repeatedly restarts the server if it crashes
A queue that permanently blocks all incoming requests
items.explanation: The event loop is what makes single-threaded concurrency possible — it picks up the next ready callback each time the currently running code yields control back.
items.reference:
Event loop
interleaves pending callbacks
one thread, many turns over time

Why: The event loop is specifically what turns a single thread into something that can serve many concurrent requests.

items.prompt: When does the event loop get a chance to run a different pending callback?
choices: Whenever the currently running code voluntarily yields control back
Only once every second, on a fixed schedule
Only when the server restarts
Never — the event loop only runs once, at server startup
items.explanation: The event loop can only pick up the next callback once the currently executing code finishes or explicitly yields — it has no way to interrupt code mid-execution.
items.reference:
Event loop
interleaves pending callbacks
one thread, many turns over time

Why: The event loop is specifically what turns a single thread into something that can serve many concurrent requests.

It refuses any request beyond a fixed hard limit
items.explanation: Because I/O waits don't occupy the thread, one thread can have many requests 'in flight' at once, each waiting on something different, without ever running more than one at a time.
items.reference:
One thread, many requests
most request time is waiting, not computing
waiting doesn't occupy the thread

Why: This is the entire premise behind non-blocking I/O scaling to large numbers of concurrent connections on one thread.
